Q: Get text content from node in React A:

For this I've lately been using fernandopasik/react-children-utilities very simply like so:

deepMap(node, (node) => ` ${onlyText(node)} `).join("")

It seems to be a well-maintained library with lots of tests. To me, this feels like something that's most appropriately outsourced to a library, as the specifics of React's internal fiber structure are complex and can change.

Some extra discussion:

React purists will say you shouldn't need to do something like this, but pragmatically it's just necessary sometimes. One case where I've needed it: I have a toast function that only runs once to set the toast content and a timeout when it will auto-dismiss. The timeout should be based on the length of the toast content, which can be a ReactNode and not just a string. We could get innerText in a useEffect after the toast is first rendered, but then a lot of effort and extra code is needed to make sure it's only done once, it keeps being associated with the right toast element as order/position changes, etc. It makes more sense to just synchronously get whatever nested static text content from children that we can.

There is renderToString from react-dom/server , but that includes a ton of extra stuff in your bundle. It also doesn't have access to all the contexts app needs (e.g. RouterProvider, QueryClientProvider , IconContext.Provider, etc.), which throws tons of errors and is simply impractical to work around because you'd have to either provide or fake all contexts somehow.

The alternative that React suggests (createRoot, flushSync, root.render) is also completely impractical. It has the same context issue. Plus, it can't be called during render. You could work around this by making it async, but this is a huge pain to do in-situ repeatedly.

Q: Construct Date - An efficient way A:

Avoid legacy date-time classes

Both the Date & Calendar classes are tragically flawed. Never use them.

Instead, use only the modern java.time classes built into Java 8+.

java.time.LocalDate

For a date-only value, just year-month-day, use the java.time.LocalDate class.

LocalDate date = LocalDate.of( 2026 , Month.JANUARY , 23 ) ;

Capturing the current date requires a time zone. For any given moment, the date varies around the globe by time zone: “tomorrow” in Tokyo Japan while simultaneously “yesterday” in Toledo Ohio US. If omitted, the JVM’s current default time zone is applied implicitly.

ZoneId zone = ZoneId.of( "America/Edmonton" ) ;  // Or, `ZoneId.systemDefault()`. 
LocalDate today = LocalDate.now( zone ) ;

The java.time classes are quite efficient, including LocalDate. No extra fields, just the year-month-day that you need for a date.

The java.time classes are based on immutable objects. So they are thread-safe by design, with no locking, etc.

The java.time classes are slated to eventually become “Value Objects” in future versions of Java. This may bring further performance enhancement through heap-flattening and scalarization. See linked document. Read Javadoc too, with caution to avoid synchronizing on these objects.

Q: Why are spaces being converted to slashes when converting a string to an array buffer? A:

JavaScript represents strings as their UTF-16 representation, a series of 16-bit (2-byte) code units. So str.charCodeAt(i) gives you the ith code unit as a number that ranges from 0x0000 (0) to 0xFFFF (65535). The operation str.charCodeAt(i) & 0xFF uses the bitwise AND operator (&) and produces a number corresponding to just the last 8 bits (1 byte) of that number, ranging from 0x00 (0) to 0xFF (255). It basically just discards the first byte of that number. If the input was already in that range, nothing changes. Otherwise you're losing information. See What does charCodeAt(...) & 0xff accomplish?.

In the specific instance where the character is NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE whose Unicode code point is 0x202F (8239), the last byte is 0x2F (47), which is the Unicode code point for SOLIDUS (forward slash). Note how this is fairly obvious when you use the hexidecimal representations of the numbers, which are directly related to the binary representations, but seems somewhat mysterious when you use the decimal representations.

That's the answer to the question as asked. You can expect all kinds of weird outputs if your inputs are outside the one-byte Basic Latin range of Unicode code points.

So, you... you definitely don't want to convert strings this way. It will turn anything outside of Basic Latin into gibberish for all consumers. It is almost certainly better to convert the string to a UTF-8-encoded representation. This will be the same for Basic Latin text. For characters outside that range you'll get a representation that is likely to be understood by the average consumer, and only gibberish to those consumers who don't speak UTF-8. And if you're using modern JavaScript, then you've already got a TextEncoder that can do this, and your stringToArrayBuffer() method could be replaced by simply

private stringToArrayBuffer(str: string) {
   return new TextEncoder().encode(str);
}

(maybe you want to reuse a TextEncoder instance? but this is already outside the scope of the question as asked.)

Q: What is the purpose of a <!DOCTYPE> declaration? A:

the doctype tells the browser what sort of rendering mode to use when rendering the web page. this can have effects on CSS layouts and cross browser development. Eric Meyer has a good article explaining it indepth.

http://www.ericmeyeroncss.com/bonus/render-mode.html

The one you point out there makes the browser view the html as XHTML 1.0 the full list of doc types allowed is here;

http://www.w3.org/QA/2002/04/valid-dtd-list.html

Q: How can I make the <!DOCTYPE> declaration change depending on the browser used? A:

Best solution is to use <!doctype html> it is a standards doctype and is now supported in all browsers since HTML5 is backwards-compatible

Plus with more and more HTML5 support being added by the browsers, it's time to prepare for the change.

Q: Why does CSS stop working once I add a <script> tag above the <!DOCTYPE> declaration? A:

The doctype declaration should be the very first thing in an HTML document, before the tag.

The doctype declaration is not an HTML tag; it is an instruction to the web browser about what version of the markup language the page is written in.

The doctype declaration refers to a Document Type Definition (DTD). The DTD specifies the rules for the markup language, so that the browsers can render the content correctly.

http://www.w3schools.com/tags/tag_DOCTYPE.asp
